needs_you.title: Which commits may follow required reviews without a re-review?
needs_you.context: The barrier only tracks implement/respond. In the initial Workflow the grade loop (format, generate) runs after the review loops, so a formatter or generator commit is pushed without any review having seen it. Landing Workflows have no review gates at all, so landing_fix (an agent editing code after approval) and agent conflict resolution during rebases land without review.
options: A. Mechanical commits (format, generate) are trusted; agent-authored commits after review (landing_fix, agent rebases) must be re-reviewed before landing.
B. Everything that moves HEAD after review requires re-review (strictest; formatter changes would trigger review rounds).
C. Today's behavior is intended: reviews cover the implementation, graders cover later fixes. Document it and record it as by design.
needs_you.recommendation: A. Mechanical steps are deterministic and already gated by graders; agent edits after approval are exactly what the barrier exists to catch. Lean then proves 'the last agent-authored commit was reviewed' for every push.
needs_you.decision: C (2026-11-20): agentic changes after approval are fine; they only happen as part of fixes and rebases. Recorded as by design.

needs_you.title: Should Epic-wide work wait for running member work, or preempt it?
needs_you.context: Merge trains and stack rebases are Epic-wide. Today an Epic-wide Workflow starts as long as no other Epic-wide Workflow is active, even while a member Job's own Workflow is running; the reconciler then cancels the member's running work (6 times in the production sample). For a stack rebase that means rebasing branches an agent may be writing to, and the cancelled member is not automatically relaunched (see 'A Job cancelled to make room for an Epic-wide Workflow is never restarted').
options: A. Epic-wide work waits: it gets a start block until no member Workflow in the Epic is active, like members already wait for it. No preemption, nothing to relaunch.
B. Epic-wide work preempts: keep cancelling member work, but cancel it before starting (not via the reconciler afterwards) and relaunch every victim when the Epic-wide Workflow finishes.
C. Keep today's behavior.
needs_you.recommendation: A. Waiting is the only option that never discards running agent work, it needs no relaunch bookkeeping, and EpicWide.lean shows it keeps the Epic exclusive under every interleaving. A stack rebase is rarely urgent enough to justify killing an implementation mid-run.
needs_you.decision: Both directions wait (2026-11-20): Epic-wide work waits until every member is idle, and member work waits until the Epic is idle. No preemption.

needs_you.title: Should Run execution be fenced by an attempt token?
needs_you.context: When a worker looks dead (stale heartbeat), recovery puts the same Run back to queued and another worker picks it up. If the original process was only stalled (long GC, network partition, laptop sleep), it can resume and continue: commit, push, call GitHub. Nothing tells it that it no longer owns the Run. The new pre-merge check (F12) only catches cancelled/finished Runs, not requeued ones.
options: A. Add an attempt counter to Run, incremented on every requeue/claim; the executor records the value it claimed and ensure_run_still_active! (already called before agent work and merges) also fails when the counter moved. Cheap, closes the gap at existing checkpoints.
B. A full lease with expiry and renewal checked before every external side effect (push, GitHub API, workspace writes).
C. Accept the risk: rely on the heartbeat threshold and the merge call's expected_sha fence.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It reuses the checkpoints that already exist and turns a stalled executor's next side effect into a clean RunEndedExternally stop. Needs a migration (one integer column), hence the question.
needs_you.decision: A (2026-11-20): an attempt counter on Run, checked at the existing ensure_run_still_active! checkpoints.

needs_you.title: What should happen to a failed Workflow's queued tail?
needs_you.context: Workflow#fail! deliberately keeps the downstream queued Steps (cancelling only orphan Runs) so 'Retry from failed step' can continue through them. The reconciler treats exactly that as abnormal and cancels the tail about a minute later (~127 repairs/week). Retry only revives cancelled Steps with no Runs, but fail! has already cancelled the queued Runs on parallel grader Steps, so a tail the reconciler cancelled is partly unrevivable. The two intents contradict each other; production recovered, with churn, through other retry paths.
options: A. A failed Workflow keeps its queued tail: the reconciler stops cancelling queued Steps of failed Workflows (it still cancels active Runs, which fail! already does). Invariant: terminal ⇒ no active Runs; failed ⇒ only dormant queued Steps.
B. fail! cancels the tail itself, and Retry revives every cancelled downstream Step (including those with cancelled Runs). Invariant: terminal ⇒ no active descendants.
C. Keep both as they are.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It matches the documented intent of fail!, needs no change to Retry, removes ~127 repairs a week, and still gives a provable invariant (no live Runs under a terminal Workflow). B is cleaner on paper but makes Retry responsible for reconstructing state it currently simply keeps.
needs_you.decision: A (2026-11-20): a failed Workflow keeps its queued tail; the reconciler stops cancelling queued Steps of failed Workflows and still cancels active Runs.

needs_you.title: May a landing-validation prefetch outlive the landing that started it?
needs_you.context: LandingValidationPrefetcher starts a child validation WorkUnit for the next landing on top of the current landing's result, once the current landing's graders pass; when it finishes, LandingValidationCache lets the next landing reuse it. The reconciler treats any active child of a finished parent as abnormal and cancels it (reconciler_spec asserts this for a succeeded auto_merge parent). In production 6 of the 7 cancellations were prefetches whose parent had just landed successfully -- the case the prefetch exists for -- so the next landing re-validated from scratch.
options: A. Yes, if the parent succeeded: the reconciler leaves a succeeded parent's LandingValidationChild children alone (it still cancels children of a failed or cancelled parent, whose base never landed). Invariant: a terminal parent's active children are exactly validation prefetches of a succeeded landing.
B. No: keep cancelling, and instead have the prefetcher re-parent the child to the next landing's unit (or to no parent) once the parent succeeds, so the state never arises.
C. Keep the current behaviour; prefetches only pay off when they finish before their parent.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It is the smallest change, keeps the prefetch's value in exactly the case it is built for, and still cancels prefetches whose base did not land. B is cleaner structurally but moves ownership logic into the prefetcher and the landing queue.
needs_you.decision: A (2026-11-20): a succeeded parent's landing-validation prefetch children may keep running; children of a failed or cancelled parent are still cancelled.

needs_you.title: After the current attempt is cancelled, is the Job failed or queued?
needs_you.context: When a running Job's current Workflow is cancelled (operator stop, cancel_stale_work, a chain cascade), JobLifecyclePropagation.cancel! marks the Job failed: 'Retry or Close'. A minute later the reconciler's Job-state plan sees [failed, latest cancelled] and moves the Job to queued, so that a stale failed pill does not suggest a current failure. For a deliberate cancellation nothing relaunches the Job, so it ends up queued with no work behind it, and a queued Job reads as 'waiting to run'. Production: JOB-9436 after an operator's stale-work repair. The two rules cannot both stand (Agreement.cancel_rules_disagree).
options: A. failed is right: the reconciler stops lifting [failed, cancelled] when the cancellation was deliberate (the existing DELIBERATE_CANCELLED_WORKFLOW_REASONS list), and keeps lifting it for cascade and conflict cancellations that are relaunched.
B. queued is right: cancel! itself returns a running Job to queued, and the Job page shows 'cancelled — nothing scheduled' for a queued Job with no work.
C. A new resting state (e.g. stopped) for an operator-stopped attempt.
needs_you.recommendation: A. failed already means 'needs an operator decision', which is exactly the situation after a deliberate stop, and the deliberate-reason list it reuses already exists for the relaunch repair. B makes queued ambiguous, and C is a new state for a rare case.
needs_you.decision: A: failed is right; the Job-state plan no longer lifts [failed, cancelled] when the cancellation was deliberate (DELIBERATE_CANCELLED_WORKFLOW_REASONS), and still lifts cascade and conflict cancellations that are relaunched.

needs_you.title: Should a landing that is blocked before its first Run ever hold the repository landing slot?
needs_you.context: The repository landing slot is the mutex every landing path checks. A landing WorkUnit takes it at creation, before its gates run. WorkUnit#block! gives it back only for an allowlist (no_capable_worker, ci_repair_disabled, and urgent_job_active before the first Run). Any other pre-start block keeps it. A manual pause is the clear case: pausing a Job whose landing Workflow has not run yet holds the slot for the whole repository until someone unpauses it. The coverage history records three production starvations, each fixed by adding one more reason to the list. Resume already re-acquires a surrendered slot before the unit can start, so surrendering never breaks mutual exclusion; the cost is that the surrendering landing can be overtaken in the queue.
options: A. Never: any block before the first Run surrenders the slot; resume re-acquires it (queue order then decides who lands first).
B. Keep the allowlist and add manual_pause and provider_availability (the indefinite ones).
C. Keep the current behaviour.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It replaces the allowlist that has starved production three times with a structural rule, and it costs nothing in mutual exclusion because resume already re-acquires; losing queue position while blocked matches how the queue already treats blocked Jobs (they do not hold it either).
needs_you.decision: A: any block before a landing's first Run surrenders the repository landing slot; the Workflow's start and resume_for_workflow! re-acquire it.

needs_you.title: Should retrying a failed dependent re-check its dependencies first?
needs_you.context: A Job only starts when its dependencies are satisfied for execution: StepDispatcher.start_workflow start-blocks it with dependency_failed (or dependency_approval_withdrawn) otherwise. A retry of a failed step reopens the existing Workflow in place (RetryFailedStepEnqueuer, used by AutoRetryJob, the Retry button and the reconciler) and never passes through start_workflow. So if dependency A was approved when dependent D started, D then failed, and A's approval was withdrawn or A failed, D's retry runs on the base the start funnel would now refuse. Rare, and not observed in production.
options: A. Re-check: RetryFailedStepEnqueuer refuses with the same dependency result the start funnel uses (reported as a wait, so auto-retry reschedules instead of giving up), and the operator's override still bypasses it.
B. Keep: a retry continues an attempt that already started legitimately; dependency regressions are handled when the dependent lands (the landing queue checks dependencies again).
C. Re-check only for automatic retries; an operator's explicit Retry proceeds.
needs_you.recommendation: B, narrowly. The landing queue re-checks dependencies before anything merges, so the worst case is wasted work on a base that may come back, not a wrong merge; A changes retry semantics for a case not seen in production. Revisit if it shows up.
needs_you.decision: B: keep. A retry continues an attempt that started legitimately; the landing queue re-checks dependencies before anything merges, so a regressed dependency costs wasted work, not a wrong merge.

needs_you.title: Should every registered MCP tool carry the authorization layer from registration, instead of from whichever path first serves it?
needs_you.context: Capability authorization (Mcp::Tools::AuthorizationSupport::ToolDispatch, which runs ScheduledAuthorization, coworker approval and actor approval) is prepended onto a tool class lazily by Mcp::Sidecar.authorize_tool, called separately by the stdio sidecar, the daemon's chat route and now (F47) the daemon's workflow route. F47 was a permission bypass because one of those paths forgot it: scheduled runs skipped the owner's rules for patch_workflow and read_artifact in persistent mode, the default. F46 was the same lazy-prepend design making wrapper order depend on process history. Any future path that serves a tool without one of the three wrappers reopens the hole silently.
options: A. Install at registration: McpToolRegistry applies authorize_tool when a tool is registered (core and plugin providers), and an architecture spec asserts every registered tool class carries the layer; the per-path calls become no-ops.
B. Keep per-path installation and add an architecture spec that every serving path (stdio sidecar, daemon chat, daemon workflow, plugin tool sets) calls authorize_tool.
C. Keep as is after F47.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It makes the guarantee structural instead of a convention every new serving path must remember, which is exactly how F47 happened; the layer is already idempotent and context-driven, so tools that need no gating pass straight through.
needs_you.decision: A: every registered tool carries the authorization layer from registration (McpToolRegistry#entry), enforced by spec/architecture/mcp_tool_authorization_spec.rb; the layer fails closed with a tool error when it cannot build the call's context.

needs_you.title: Should auto-merge refuse to merge when no validated base was recorded?
needs_you.context: Before calling GitHub's merge, auto-merge compares the live base head with job.mergeability_base_sha, the base the mergeability preflight recorded before the landing graders ran. F49 made an unreadable live base defer instead of merging. A blank recorded base still skips the check and merges. The preflight records the PR's base from GitHub's payload on every landing, so a blank value means GitHub sent no base SHA, or the Job reached auto_merge without a preflight. Not observed in production.
options: A. Fail closed: a blank recorded base defers landing for a re-check, like an unreadable live base, so the next preflight records it.
B. Keep: a blank recorded base means there is nothing to compare, and the landing validation manifest still binds the head SHA.
C. Compare with the manifest's base_sha instead of the Job column, and fail closed when both are blank.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It closes the last path in the check that merges without knowing the base, at the cost of one deferral in a state that should not occur. C is better long-term but changes which record is authoritative.
needs_you.decision: A (2026-11-21): a blank recorded validated base defers landing for a re-check, like an unreadable live base.

needs_you.title: Should the in-place step retry budget be per Step or per Job?
needs_you.context: worker_died and git_transport_transient failures on deterministic Steps (graders, mechanical steps) are retried in place by Runs::LifecyclePropagation. That path counts only attempts on the same Step's Runs, while the reconciler's retry repair counts every attempt of the Job with the same provider and classification. In-place attempts do count against the job-wide budget, so the reconciler cannot add more after a Step exhausts its own, but each Step gets a fresh in-place budget. A GitHub outage during a 100-grader landing fan-out can therefore schedule up to 3 delayed retries per grader (300 for one classification) instead of 3 for the Job. Bounded, and introduced three days ago without a stated rationale; not observed in production.
options: A. Keep per Step: fan-out graders fail independently, and a per-Job budget would let one flaky grader exhaust retries for its siblings.
B. Per Job for git_transport_transient, per Step for worker_died: a transport outage affects every Step alike, so one job-wide budget is enough, while worker loss is per host.
C. Per Job for both, matching the reconciler.
needs_you.recommendation: B. A transport outage is one event, and the job-wide count already exists (budget_scope_for); worker_died keeps its higher per-Step limit, where independence is real.
needs_you.decision: A (2026-11-21): keep the per-Step in-place budget. Infrastructure failures should fail work as rarely as possible while runaway loops stay bounded; each Step's budget is bounded (step_bound) and in-place attempts still count against the job-wide reconciler budget.

needs_you.title: Should a plugin tool be able to declare approval_effect for itself?
needs_you.context: A tool marked approval_effect skips the generic 'ask' approval because its only mutation is creating the owner's real confirmation card (documented in the Coworkers docs); policy is still evaluated and a deny still refuses it. For core tools the flag is set in McpToolRegistry, or derived when the tool is a registered pending action. A plugin's tool-set definition can also set approval_effect: true (Mcp::CoworkerToolCatalog), and nothing checks that such a tool really creates a confirmation card, so a plugin tool could declare it and run on 'ask' with no confirmation. Today only the Coworkers plugin's own spawn-chat tools use it, and they do create cards. DOC-44: 'Plugin-contributed capabilities cannot bypass the evaluator.'
options: A. Honour approval_effect only for core-registered tools and tools that are registered pending actions; a plugin definition's flag is ignored unless the plugin registers the pending action it creates.
B. Keep honouring plugin declarations, and add a contract spec that every tool declaring approval_effect returns a pending action when invoked.
C. Keep as is: plugins are trusted code reviewed like core.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It makes the exemption derived rather than declared, the same way pending-action tools already are, and costs nothing for today's tools (the spawn-chat tools can register their pending actions).
needs_you.decision: A, and check it (2026-11-21). Implementation detail pending: the only plugin tools that declare approval_effect (the Coworkers spawn tools) create their card themselves, through AuthorizationSupport.pending_coworker_plugin_approval, with normalized arguments. Requiring a registered pending action means giving those tools pending-action classes; letting the generic layer create the card instead risks a second card on the approved re-run, because the arguments differ. Needs a choice between the two.

needs_you.title: Should a runtime database error make disabled plugins' providers callable?
needs_you.context: Syrus::PluginRegistry.providers_for reads plugin enablement from PluginRecord. On any ActiveRecord error it returns every registered plugin's providers, disabled and unhealthy ones included (pinned by 'returns all plugins when the database is unavailable'). That exists so asset precompile and boot work before the database does. At runtime the same rescue turns a transient error (a lock-wait timeout, a dropped connection) into every disabled plugin's contribution being callable for that call: an execution backend, an approval provider, a repository content provider. PluginRegistry.health falls back the same way.
options: A. Fall back to the last enablement set this process read successfully; return every plugin only when none was ever read (precompile, first boot).
B. Fail closed at runtime: no plugin providers on a database error, keep the all-plugins fallback only when no database is configured.
C. Keep as is.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It keeps precompile and boot working, keeps a running instance's behaviour stable through a blip, and never activates a plugin the operator disabled. B is safer still but turns a transient error into every plugin vanishing for that call.
needs_you.decision: Retry until there is a definite answer (2026-11-21): never treat installed plugins as enabled. Implemented as F69: defaults for a missing database or table, every plugin only for an asset build, otherwise retried and then EnablementUnavailable; the Installer keeps its effects when enablement cannot be read.

needs_you.title: Should an enabled but unhealthy plugin keep its kinds installed for work already in flight?
needs_you.context: KindRegistry installs kinds from PluginRegistry.providers_for(:workflow_kinds), which keeps only enabled and healthy plugins. A plugin that turns degraded, failed or incompatible after boot (a broken dependency, which F60 now propagates; a failed load after an upgrade) loses its trigger and step kinds with no disable action to guard. Its queued or running workflows then raise WorkDefinitions::UnknownKind on cancellation cascades, and their step handlers no longer resolve. F61 only guards operator disables.
options: A. Keep the kind metadata (entries and WorkDefinition) of every installed plugin resolvable for existing rows, and let only new work require an enabled and healthy owner. Unhealthy work then fails closed when it next tries to start a step, but can always be cancelled.
B. Have the reconciler cancel active work whose kind is no longer installed, with a clear 'plugin unavailable' reason.
C. Keep as is: an unhealthy plugin's in-flight work stays stuck until it is healthy again.
needs_you.recommendation: A. Cancellation and display need only metadata, not the plugin's code paths. It matches F61's create-only validation, and it keeps the 'withheld providers are never called' rule for anything that starts work. B loses work that a plugin fix would have resumed.
needs_you.decision: A (2026-11-21). Implemented as F74: existing rows resolve their definition from the installed plugin whatever its state (WorkDefinitions.for_existing), or the neutral Unavailable; launches still need an enabled and healthy owner.

needs_you.title: Should Coding Mode `!` shell commands be contained when contained chat execution is required?
needs_you.context: Under contained_chat_execution: required, ChatTurnJob runs the chat agent through a fail-closed ChatWorkloadPolicy, so no agent process runs on the worker. ChatShellCommandExecutor::Coding runs the operator's `!` commands through ProcessRunner with no workload policy, so they still run on the worker host, in the persistent ChatWorkspace checkout the contained agent writes to. An `!npm test` or `!bin/rspec` therefore executes code the contained agent wrote, outside the container.
options: A. Attach ChatWorkloadPolicy to Coding Mode `!` commands too, so under required they run in the container or fail with 'no execution backend'.
B. Keep `!` commands on the worker (the operator typed them), and say so in the contained-chat setting's help text.
C. Keep as is.
needs_you.recommendation: A. The containment boundary is about where agent-influenced code executes, and the checkout is agent-written. Under 'preferred' nothing changes, because an unavailable backend still falls back to the worker.
needs_you.decision: New option (2026-11-21): when containment is required, Coding Mode ! commands are disabled with an explanation. Implemented: 403 containment_required with a translated explanation, refused again at run time, Local Mode unaffected.

needs_you.title: Drop the two orphaned operator briefing tables?
needs_you.context: db/schema.rb declares operator_briefing_review_findings and operator_briefing_workflow_notable_changes, but no migration creates them and no code uses them. The removed detector pipeline wrote them, and its removal edited the original migration instead of adding a drop. A later schema dump copied them back. Fresh installs build them from schema.rb, databases that ran the original migration still hold their rows, and PluginPurge can never remove them. A drop migration deletes whatever rows production still has.
options: A. Add an idempotent operator_briefing migration that drops both tables (drop_table ..., if_exists: true) and remove them from schema.rb and the spec's pending list.
B. Only remove them from schema.rb, so fresh installs stop creating them, and leave existing databases alone.
C. Keep as is.
needs_you.recommendation: A. The rows came from a pipeline that no longer exists and nothing reads them. B alone comes back the next time someone dumps the schema from a database that still has the tables, which is how they came back the first time.
needs_you.decision: A (2026-11-21): delete the leftovers. Implemented: an idempotent drop migration in operator_briefing, both removed from schema.rb, and no pending list in the spec.

needs_you.title: How should a worker without a plugin handle a Run of that plugin's step kind?
needs_you.context: Workers heartbeat their plugin-set digest and plugin list, but routing (RunQueueResolver) ignores them, and no work records the plugin set it needs. During a fleet plugin rollout, or for a fleet installation limited to some roles, a worker that lacks the plugin can claim a Run of the plugin's step kind. RunJob then raises in Steps.handler_for, and the step fails terminally, even though a worker that has the plugin could run it. Bundled plugins are unaffected: they load everywhere and declare no roles.
options: A. Treat the owning plugin as a placement requirement: RunQueueResolver asks for a live worker whose heartbeat lists the plugin that contributes the step kind, and otherwise blocks the start as no_capable_worker, the same way an OS or toolchain requirement does.

B. In RunJob, when the step kind is unknown on this process but known to the instance, release the Run back to the queue with a bounded deferral instead of failing it, and fail only once no live worker reports the plugin.
C. Keep as is: a fleet plugin rollout can fail in-flight steps of that plugin's kinds.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It reuses the existing capability-routing contract and the no_capable_worker diagnosis, so a blocked start explains itself. B is smaller, but it spins on a worker that will never have the plugin.
needs_you.decision: Prevent it (2026-11-21). Implemented as F73: a worker that does not provide a step's kind hands the Run back (30 s, up to 20 times) instead of failing it, and an unknown kind's Step can fail cleanly. Per-plugin queue routing, which would avoid the hand-backs, is a larger change and not done.

needs_you.title: Should the Host API give plugins the enabled-and-healthy plugin set?
needs_you.context: Two bundled plugins resolve their own contributions by reading manifests: ConnectedAccounts::ProviderRegistry (OAuth provider declarations, which need the contributing plugin's name) and PluginRuntime::DesiredServiceCollection (supervised services). Both filter with manifest.enabled? only, so a degraded or failed contributor's OAuth provider or service stays active. That is the gap F62 and F66 closed in core. The declared Host API (lib/syrus/host/public_apis.rb) promises register, providers_for and extension_point? on PluginRegistry, and says health is not promised, so the plugins cannot apply the core rule themselves.
options: A. Add a public PluginRegistry.active_plugins (manifests that are enabled and healthy, the providers_for set) to the Host API, and switch both registries to it.
B. Add a public providers_with_owner_for(point) that returns [plugin_name, provider] pairs from the health-aware hosted path, and have both registries use that instead of reading manifests.
C. Keep as is: plugin-side registries own their own filtering.
needs_you.recommendation: B. It keeps plugins out of manifest internals and makes the health rule impossible to forget, because there is no enabled-only path left to reach for. A adds a second public notion of 'enabled'.
needs_you.decision: B (2026-11-21): add one. Implemented as F72: public PluginRegistry.providers_with_owner_for on the health-aware hosted path; Connected Accounts and Plugin Runtime use it.

needs_you.title: What should the client guarantee when an app event is genuinely lost?
needs_you.context: When the client sees a sequence gap on the user channel (10, then 12), it refreshes only the queries of the event after the gap (recoverEventResourceContinuity). The lost event's resource is unknown, so it stays stale until an unrelated reconnect, focus refetch or later event. F67 now applies late deliveries, so a gap that closes on its own needs no recovery at all. Only a sequence that never arrives needs one.
options: A. Wait a short grace period (about 2s) for the missing sequences to arrive late. Any still missing then triggers recoverAppEventContinuity, the reconnect sweep of active continuity queries, which defers for hidden tabs as it already does.
B. Keep a short replayable server-side event window per user and request the missing range on a gap.
C. Keep the targeted refresh, and state the weaker guarantee: the stale resource converges on the next reconnect or focus refetch.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It needs no server change and sweeps only on a genuine loss. revision_gap_recoveries already measures how often that happens, so the cost is visible before and after. B is the strongest option, but it adds server state and a new endpoint.
needs_you.decision: A (2026-11-21): wait about 2 s for late deliveries, then sweep. Implemented as F71.

needs_you.title: Should an open Job subscription stop when the user loses access to the Job?
needs_you.context: JobChannel authorizes with Job.visible_to only when a client subscribes, and then streams from one shared job_resource:<id> stream. Removing a user's repository membership, or narrowing Job visibility, does not end open subscriptions. Until the tab reconnects, that user keeps receiving the Job's Workflow, Step and Run field patches (state, timestamps, PR title, summary, cost). ChatChannel does not have this problem after F68, because it uses per-user streams whose recipients are recomputed on each broadcast.
options: A. Move JobChannel to per-user streams like ChatChannel, with recipients recomputed from Job.visible_to on each broadcast. This costs one visibility query per Job broadcast.
B. Keep the shared stream, but have every membership or visibility change disconnect that user's open JobChannel subscriptions (ActionCable remote_connections), so they must re-authorize.
C. Accept it: visibility revocation takes effect on the next reconnect, and the patches carry no secrets.
needs_you.recommendation: B. It keeps the shared stream, which matters because Job events are the high-churn ones, and makes revocation immediate at the single place access changes. A is simpler to reason about, but it multiplies the cost of every Job broadcast.
needs_you.decision: Prevent it (2026-11-21). Implemented as F70, by rechecking Job.visible_to on delivery (cached 10 s) rather than disconnect hooks, because visibility has more inputs than any hook list would cover.

needs_you.title: Should an expired replication lease stop protecting a backup from deletion?
needs_you.context: LocalBackups::Retention never deletes a backup that has an uploading replication. Replication leases last six hours, are never renewed, and nothing expires them, so a replication whose worker died stays 'uploading' until the same destination re-pins after expiry. If the destination never comes back, for example because it was removed mid-upload, the backup is protected from retention and capacity reclamation forever. Letting expiry lift the protection would allow deleting an artifact under an upload that runs longer than the lease.
options: A. Keep deletion conservative, and add a sweep that marks a replication 'failed' once its lease has expired and its destination is no longer configured, so only an abandoned upload is released.
B. Treat an uploading replication as protecting the backup only while its lease is active, and renew the lease while a long upload is running.
C. Keep as is: an abandoned upload pins its backup until an operator deletes it.
needs_you.recommendation: A. It never deletes under a live or recoverable upload, and it releases exactly the case that cannot recover on its own.

needs_you.title: Should recovery preflight block when it cannot establish compatibility, rather than warn?
needs_you.context: LocalBackups::Recovery preflight fails on a known mismatch: a different database adapter or major version, an older destination application, or a required plugin missing or at another version. But it only warns when information is missing: the destination's application version, database adapter or database version not supplied, no compatibility range in the bundle, or versions that do not parse. Warnings need no acknowledgement, so preflight reports 'ready' and a restore can proceed into a destination whose compatibility was never established. Restore replaces the database.
options: A. Treat every unknown as a failure, and allow it only with an explicit operator flag (like the existing --break-glass-no-safety-backup), named after what is unknown.
B. Keep warnings, but require the operator to acknowledge the listed warnings by passing their codes before a restore starts.
C. Keep as is.
needs_you.recommendation: A, in line with NY13: an unknown is not a pass, and restore is destructive. The break-glass flag keeps the empty-instance and development cases possible on purpose.
